stem: A client has aphasia after a stroke. Which communication approach by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Use short adult-level sentences, speak at a comfortable pace and volume, allow extra response time, and use writing, pictures, or gestures when helpful.
options.B: Speak loudly and rapidly so the client receives more information before becoming frustrated by the communication difficulty.
options.C: Direct questions primarily to the family because aphasia indicates that the client is unable to understand spoken language or participate in decisions.
options.D: Avoid alternative communication methods so the client must practice spoken language during every interaction until verbal fluency returns.

rationale: ASHA guidance for adults with communication disorders recommends simple but adult language, slower speech, short sentences, adequate time to communicate, and multimodal supports such as pictures, writing, and gestures when useful. Aphasia does not automatically imply cognitive impairment or absent comprehension. Therefore, A is best. B adds unnecessary loudness and speed, C wrongly assumes incapacity and bypasses the client, and D removes compensatory communication methods that can support effective participation.
educational_objective: Communicate with a client who has post-stroke aphasia by allowing time and using clear adult-level language plus individualized multimodal supports without assuming cognitive incapacity.
source_document_title: Aphasia — ASHA Practice Portal; Tips for Communicating With Adults Who Have a Speech or Language Disorder
source_locator: ASHA Practice Portal → Aphasia → Differential Diagnosis: aphasia does not imply cognitive deficits; Partner Approaches → Conversational Coaching and Supported Conversation for Adults With Aphasia: communication partners may use drawing, gesturing, cueing, confirming, summarizing and multimodal communication. ASHA communication tips → 'To help someone understand you better': keep voice at a comfortable level, use simple but adult words, slow speech, short sentences, and pictures/gestures/writing; 'To help someone express themselves better': give time to communicate and invite drawing, writing, pointing, or gesturing as needed.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports adult-level simplified language, appropriate pace/volume, extra response time, multimodal communication supports, and avoidance of the assumption that aphasia means cognitive incapacity.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Appendix A → Psychosocial Integrity → Therapeutic Communication, printed PDF page 33/file page 37: assess verbal and nonverbal client communication needs; allow time to communicate with the client; use therapeutic communication techniques; evaluate effectiveness of communication. Related Psychosocial Integrity activity statements also include recognizing nonverbal cues and providing appropriate care for cognitive/sensory alterations.
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — therapeutic communication adapted to a client with post-stroke aphasia
correction_summary: Rebuilt and reclassified the source item from Basic Care and Comfort to Psychosocial Integrity because the tested nursing construct is therapeutic communication. Replaced the generic ASHA locator with exact current ASHA communication-partner guidance, added the important distinction that aphasia does not automatically imply cognitive impairment, and rewrote distractors around realistic errors in pace/volume, client participation, and multimodal support.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current ASHA Practice Portal and ASHA communication guidance, appropriate authoritative specialty sources for aphasia and communication-partner strategies.
audit_findings.currentness: The ASHA Aphasia Practice Portal and communication-tip resource are active current resources at the audit date and incorporate contemporary partner and multimodal communication approaches.

claim_by_claim.stem: Aphasia after stroke is a clinically coherent communication impairment requiring adaptation of nurse-client interaction.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because ASHA supports simple adult language, slower/clear speech, short sentences, extra time, and multimodal tools such as writing, pictures and gestures.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because ASHA advises a comfortable voice level and slower speech rather than unnecessary loudness or rapid delivery.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because aphasia does not itself establish cognitive impairment or inability to participate; communication should be supported with the client rather than automatically redirected to family.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because ASHA partner and multimodal approaches explicitly use gestures, writing, pictures and other compensatory modalities to support communication.
claim_by_claim.rationale: Contains no unsupported assumption about aphasia subtype, prognosis, recovery duration, or mandatory communication device.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to nurse communication with a post-stroke client who has aphasia.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests the common error of treating a language disorder like hearing loss; C tests assumption of incapacity; D tests inappropriate restriction of compensatory modalities. Each is realistic, distinct, and source-addressable.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A combines source-supported pacing, language level, time allowance and multimodal support. No alternative contains a defensible equivalent communication strategy.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe complete communication approaches; the keyed response is not identifiable by grammar or option structure alone.
audit_findings.blueprint: Psychosocial Integrity is a stronger classification than Basic Care and Comfort because the 2026 NCSBN Test Plan explicitly lists assessment of communication needs, allowance of communication time, and therapeutic communication techniques under Psychosocial Integrity.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited after reclassification and challenged whether expressive aphasia could justify directing questions to family, whether simple language risks infantilization, and whether spoken-language practice should replace compensatory methods. The final key explicitly uses adult-level language and individualized multimodal supports, consistent with ASHA and NCSBN. No unresolved conflict remains.
